# [2401.07883] The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator

[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.07883) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1)
> Abstract:Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has become one of the most popular paradigms for enabling LLMs to access external data, and also as a mechanism for grounding to mitigate against hallucinations. When implementing RAG you can face several challenges like effective integration of retrieval models, efficient representation learning, data diversity, computational efficiency optimization, evaluation, and quality of text generation. Given all these challenges, every day a new technique to improve RAG appears, making it unfeasible to experiment with all combinations for your problem. In this context, this paper presents good practices to implement, optimize, and evaluate RAG for the Brazilian Portuguese language, focusing on the establishment of a simple pipeline for inference and experiments. We explored a diverse set of methods to answer questions about the first Harry Potter book. To generate the answers we used the OpenAI's gpt-4, gpt-4-1106-preview, gpt-3.5-turbo-1106, and Google's Gemini Pro. Focusing on the quality of the retriever, our approach achieved an improvement of MRR@10 by 35.4% compared to the baseline. When optimizing the input size in the application, we observed that it is possible to further enhance it by 2.4%. Finally, we present the complete architecture of the RAG with our recommendations. As result, we moved from a baseline of 57.88% to a maximum relative score of 98.61%.

*Leonardo Avila Rodrigo Castaldoni Pedro Gengo Celio Larcher Marcos Piau Pablo Costa Vinicius Caridá

###### Abstract

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has become one of the most popular paradigms for enabling LLMs to access external data, and also as a mechanism for grounding to mitigate against hallucinations. When implementing RAG you can face several challenges like effective integration of retrieval models, efficient representation learning, data diversity, computational efficiency optimization, evaluation, and quality of text generation. Given all these challenges, every day a new technique to improve RAG appears, making it unfeasible to experiment with all combinations for your problem. In this context, this paper presents good practices to implement, optimize, and evaluate RAG for the Brazilian Portuguese language, focusing on the establishment of a simple pipeline for inference and experiments. We explored a diverse set of methods to answer questions about the first Harry Potter book. To generate the answers we used the OpenAI’s gpt-4, gpt-4-1106-preview, gpt-3.5-turbo-1106, and Google’s Gemini Pro. ## 1 Introduction

The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has changed the way we approach Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications. Their ability to answer different user queries in different domains allow these models to show a notable performance in a wide range of tasks like translation, summarizing, question answering, and many others [[1](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib1 "")]. However, there are a lot of open challenges when it comes to problems that require answers based on updated information, and external data, that were not available in the training data.

In order to overcome this challenge, a technique called Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) [[2](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib2 "")] was developed. This approach aims to solve the limitation of the need for external data, by fetching and incorporating this information in the prompt. With this, the model can generate more cohesive answers about subjects and data not seen during the training, decreasing the occurrence of hallucinations [[3](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib3 "")]. Nevertheless, this approach adds a new layer of challenges since it requires the development of a trustworthy retriever pipeline, given that the quality of the final answer can be highly affected if the retrieved text is not relevant to the user query [[4](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib4 "")].

The landscape of RAG is rapidly expanding, with a constant influx of new papers introducing diverse implementations [[5](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib5 "")]. Each of these variants proposes technical modifications or enhancements, such as different retrieval mechanisms, augmentation techniques, or fine-tuning methodologies. This proliferation, while a testament to the field’s dynamism, presents a substantial challenge for AI practitioners. The task of methodically experimenting with, and critically evaluating, each variant’s performance, scalability, and applicability becomes increasingly complex.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive series of experiments focused on the application of RAG specifically tailored for Brazilian Portuguese. Our research delves into evaluating various retrieval techniques, including both sparse and dense retrievers. Additionally, we explore two chunking strategies (naive and sentence window) to optimize the integration of retrieved information into the generation process. We also investigate the impact of the positioning of documents within the prompt, analyzing how this influences the overall quality and relevance of the generated content. Finally, our experiments extend to comparing the performance of different LLMs, notably GPT-4 and Gemini, in their ability to effectively incorporate the retrieved information and produce coherent, contextually accurate responses. This paper aims to provide valuable insights and practical guidelines for implementing RAG in Brazilian Portuguese.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 1) we propose a methodology to prepare a dataset in a format that allows quantifying the quality of the different steps in an RAG system. 2) We proposed a metric (maximum relative score) that allow us to direct quantify the existent gap between each approach and a perfect RAG system. 3) We discuss and compare different implementations, showing good practices and optimizations that can be used when developing a RAG system.

## 2 Data Preparation

The chosen dataset was the first Harry Potter book in its Brazilian Portuguese version. This choice is motivated since it is a well known book, and both the Gemini Pro and OpenAI models can answer general questions on the subject. Following, a dataset consisting of questions and corresponding answers was developed, with both question and answer generated by the gpt-4 model and based on a reference chunk.

## 3 How to Evaluate

The contextual comparison of two text samples is not a straightforward task. For instance, despite the sentence<!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="{}_{1}=" intent=":literal" id="S3.p1.m1"><semantics><mrow><msub><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{1}=</annotation></semantics></math> --> 1={}_{1}= "Brazil has won 5 FIFA World Cup titles.", and sentence<!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="{}_{2}=" display="inline" id="S3.p1.m2"><semantics><mrow><msub><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{2}=</annotation></semantics></math> --> 2={}_{2}= "Brazil is the five-time champion of the FIFA World Cup." (both sentences translated into English for convenience) convey the same meaning, traditional metrics such as BLEU [[7](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib7 "")] and ROUGE [[8](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib8 "")] score may not be able to capture such similarity. Specifically, for the example cited:

- •     BLEU score <!-- MathML: <math alttext="[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.33" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>sentence</mtext><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>sentence</mtext><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.33</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.33</annotation></semantics></math> --> [sentence1,sentence2]=0.33[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.33

- •     ROUGE score <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.22" id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msub><mtext>sentence</mtext><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mtext>sentence</mtext><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.22</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.22</annotation></semantics></math> --> [sentence1,sentence2]=0.22[\text{sentence}_{1},\text{sentence}_{2}]=0.22

Therefore, an approach widely used in the literature is to employ gpt-4 to provide a score based on a given prompt, a concept similar to what was done in the G-Eval work [[9](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib9 "")]. In this work, a scoring system divided into <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="5" id="S3.p3.m1"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> --> 55 categories to compare two texts was devised, with scores defined as following (translated into English for convenience):

- •     score 1: The answer has no relation to the reference.

- •     score 3: The answer has little relevance but is not aligned with the reference.

- •     score 5: The answer has moderate relevance but contains inaccuracies.

- •     score 7: The answer is aligned with the reference but has minor omissions.

- •     score 10: The answer is completely accurate and aligns perfectly with the reference.

The prompt used in the evaluation is shown in Appendix [A](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#A1 "Appendix A PROMPTS ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"). Our approach uses a one-shot technique for each scoring category. Although, we believe that the evaluation could become more robust and deterministic with the addition of more few-shot examples for each scoring category, these possible variations were not explored in this work.

### 3.1 Relative Maximum Score

In order to assess performance variation for the followings experiments, we created a metric called the relative maximum score, which corresponds to the score given by a model when evaluating the correct combination of question and chunk for all pairs of a given dataset. Through this approach, it is possible to obtain the maximum score that an evaluated LLM could reach for a RAG system.

The Table [1](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Relative Maximum Score ‣ 3 How to Evaluate ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") presents results for the custom dataset created in Section [2](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S2 "2 Data Preparation ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"), by using different LLMs to generate the answer and the gpt-4 score system previously defined.

## 4 Introductory Experiments

Additionally, we will apply techniques of lower complexity and compare the results with the baseline. It’s worth noting that we did not explore prompt engineering techniques, although we are aware that prompt engineering has a direct impact on performance, as demonstrated in [[10](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib10 "")].

### 4.1 Baseline: no context

We are aware that LLMs are trained on a massive dataset that covers virtually the entire web. This circumstance, coupled with the popularity of the Harry Potter universe, forms a robust hypothesis for testing questions in isolation on OpenAI models. ## 5 Advanced Experiments

The studies and experiments outlined in section [4](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S4 "4 Introductory Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") have shown unsatisfactory performance, marked by a degradation of at least <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="20\%" id="S5.p1.m1"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 20%20\% compared to the peak relative performance. Therefore, in this section, we explore various retrieval approaches for the RAG, recognizing that the quality of the retriever is a crucial factor in enhancing performance for this type of problem. We conducted an evaluation covering both sparse and dense search, a hybrid method, and even a multi-stage architecture using a reranker.

In pursuit of code debugging flexibility and easier customization at each stage, we chose not to utilize an RAG framework (like LangChain or Llama-Index). For a comprehensive guide on debugging RAG and more details about retrieval systems, refer to [[20](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib20 "")] and [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib21 "")].

### 5.1 Retrievers

When deploying retrieval systems, it is essential to achieve a balance between “effectiveness” (How good are the results returned?) and “efficiency” (How much time it takes to return the results? or How much resources are used in terms of disk/RAM/GPU?). This balance ensures that latency, result quality, and computational budget remain within our application’s required limits. This work will exclusively focus on effectiveness measures to quantify the retrievers methods quality.

In our retriever experiments, the evaluation strategy centers around assessing how well the retriever performs in retrieving relevant information based on each given query <!-- MathML: <math alttext="q_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.p2.m1"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> --> qiq_{i}. To achieve this, we employ the concept of recall. It is defined as the fraction of the relevant documents for a given query <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="q_{i}" id="S5.SS1.p2.m2"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> --> qiq_{i} that are successfully retrieved in a ranked list <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="R" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.p2.m3"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> --> RR [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib21 "")]. This metric is based on binary relevance judgments, assuming that documents are either relevant or not [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib21 "")]. In this paper, each chunk is considered a document and only the respective chunk <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="d_{i}" id="S5.SS1.p2.m4"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> --> did_{i} is considered relevant to the query <!-- MathML: <math alttext="q_{i}" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S5.SS1.p2.m5"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> --> qiq_{i}. While recall is easy to interpret, it does not consider the specific rank positions in which the relevant chunk appears in <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="R" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.p2.m6"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> --> RR.

To overcome this limitation, we introduce Reciprocal Rank (RR) into our analysis. In this metric, the rank of the first relevant document to the query in <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="R" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.p3.m1"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> --> RR is used to compute the RR score [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib21 "")]. Therefore, Reciprocal Rank offers a more nuanced evaluation by assigning a higher value when the relevant chunk is returned in the early positions of our retrievers given the respective query.

Recall and Reciprocal Rank were evaluated at a specific cutoff so the measures are presented as R@k and MRR@k. For each query, its results are evaluated and their mean serves as an aggregated measure of effectiveness of a given retriever method. The retrievers are introduced below.

In the category of sparse retrievers, we emphasize the BM25, a technique grounded in statistical weighting to assess relevance between search terms and documents. BM25 employs a scoring function that takes into account term frequency and document length, offering an efficient approach for retrieving pertinent information and is typically used as a strong baseline. However, it is exact-match based and can be powerless when query and document are relevant to each other but has no common words.

On the other hand, when exploring dense retrievers, we often encounter approaches based on the called bi-encoder design [[22](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib22 "")]. The bi-encoder independently encodes queries and documents, creating separate vector representations before calculating similarity. An advantage of this approach is that it can be initialized ‘offline’: document embeddings can be precomputed, leaving only the query embedding being calculated at search time, reducing latency.

The hybrid search technique aims to leverage the best of both sparse and dense search approaches. Given a question, both searches are conducted in parallel, generating two lists of candidate documents to answer it. The challenge then lies in combining the two results in the best possible way, ensuring that the final hybrid list surpasses the individual searches. Essentially, we can conceptualize it as a voting system, where each searcher casts a vote on the relevance of a document to a given query, and in the end, the opinions are combined to produce a better result.

The multi-stage search architecture is based on the retrieve-and-rerank pipeline. In the first stage, a retriever with good recall is typically used to perform an initial filtering of the documents to be returned. From this narrowed-down list, these candidate documents are then sent to a second stage, which involves higher computational complexity, to rerank them and enhance the final effectiveness of the system.

Next, we provide more details about each retriever used.

#### 5.1.1 BM25

Due to the user-friendly nature of BM25, its inclusion as a retriever method is always a welcome addition in RAG evaluations. A study that aligns with the same reasoning, albeit for a different application, can be found in [[23](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib23 "")], which illustrates the benefits of employing this algorithm to establish a robust baseline. Given that our data shares similarities with the SQuAD dataset, it is expected that many words from the query would be present in the chunk, contributing to the favorable effectiveness of BM25.

#### 5.1.5 Reranker

The fundamental idea underlying multi-stage ranking is to divide document ranking into a sequence of stages. After an initial retrieval, which usually involves a sparse retriever or dense retriever, each subsequent stage re-evaluates and reranks the set of candidates forwarded from the preceding stage. Figure [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 5.1.5 Reranker ‣ 5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") represents a multi-stage pipeline where Pyserini BM25 performs the first stage and the candidate chunks are then re-evaluated by the reranker. After that, the final reranked list called retrieved chunks is presented as final result formed by <!-- MathML: <math alttext="k" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S5.SS1.SSS5.p1.m1"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> --> kk chunks.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/reranker.png)Figure 9: Reranker Pipeline

Transformers-based models are commonly employed as rerankers, leveraging their capability to enhance the effectiveness of information retrieval systems by capturing intricate relationships and contextual information within documents and queries.

The initial utilization of transformers within a multi-stage ranking framework was presented in the study [[28](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib28 "")]. Their proposed model, known as monoBERT, transforms the ranking process into a relevance classification problem. It achieves this by sorting texts based on the conditional probability <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="P(\text{Relevant}=1\,|\,d_{i};q)" display="inline" id="S5.SS1.SSS5.p3.m1"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext>Relevant</mtext><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0.170em">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(\text{Relevant}=1\,|\,d_{i};q)</annotation></semantics></math> --> P⁡(Relevant=1|di;q)P(\text{Relevant}=1\,|\,d_{i};q), where <!-- MathML: <math alttext="q" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S5.SS1.SSS5.p3.m2"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> --> qq is the query and <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="d_{i}" intent=":literal" id="S5.SS1.SSS5.p3.m3"><semantics><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> --> did_{i} represents documents [[21](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib21 "")]. The model simultaneously processes both queries and documents. This simultaneous processing leads to a more enriched interaction between them, often resulting in improved effectiveness [[29](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib29 "")], [[30](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib30 "")]. However, this neural models have a substantial number of parameters and the scoring of query-document pairs occurs at inference time. This, in turn, increases computational costs and latency. This kind of model is also known by cross-encoder. Refer to Figure [10](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 5.1.5 Reranker ‣ 5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") for an illustration of the query-document pair processing.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/cross_encoder.png)Figure 10: Cross-Encoder

In the other hand, monoT5 is a sequence-to-sequence reranker [[31](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib31 "")] that uses T5 models [[32](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib32 "")] to generate relevance scores between a pair of query and document. T5 models treat all tasks as text-to-text, requiring some adaptations for the query/document similarity task. During training, the format 'Query: {query} Document: {document} Relevant:' is used, with labels yes if the document is relevant to the query, and no otherwise. At inference time, the same format as the training data is used to format pairs of queries and documents to feed the model, and a single-token greedy decode is performed. The score is then obtained by calculating the softmax value considering only the tokens no and yes, and selecting the value corresponding to the yes token. Note that the tokens no and yes are the tokens used in the version provided by [[33](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib33 "")], but the publication that introduced the monoT5 architecture, [[31](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib31 "")], uses the tokens false and true. Figure [11](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 5.1.5 Reranker ‣ 5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") contains an illustration of the monoT5 architecture’s inference process.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/monot5.png)Figure 11: monoT5’s inference process

## 6 Conclusions

The implementation of RAG systems faces challenges such as the effective integration of retrieval models, efficient representation learning, the diversity of data, the optimization of computational efficiency, evaluation, and text generation quality. Faced with these constantly evolving obstacles, this article proposes best practices for the implementation, optimization, and evaluation of RAG on a Brazilian Portuguese dataset, focusing on a simplified pipeline for inference and experimentation.

So far, we have introduced the main components and methods along with their results and gaps. In this section, we will discuss key points that contribute to the performance improvement in RAG applications. We will start by discussing the relationship between the quality of the retriever and the achieved performance, in which our approach showed a significant improvement of MRR@10 by <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="35.4\%" id="S6.p2.m1"><semantics><mrow><mn>35.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">35.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 35.4%35.4\% compared to the baseline. Next, we will address the impact of input size on performance. In this domain, we observed that it is possible to enhance the best information retrieval strategy by <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="2.4\%" intent=":literal" id="S6.p2.m2"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 2.4%2.4\% through input size optimization. Finally, we will present the complete architecture of RAG with our recommendations. When evaluating the final accuracy of our approach, we reached <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="98.61\%" display="inline" id="S6.p2.m3"><semantics><mrow><mn>98.61</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98.61\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 98.61%98.61\%, representing an improvement of <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="40.73" intent=":literal" id="S6.p2.m4"><semantics><mn>40.73</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40.73</annotation></semantics></math> --> 40.7340.73 in less degradation score compared to the baseline.

### 6.1 Retriever Score versus Performance

As mentioned in section [5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.SS1 "5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"), the performance of information/chunk retrieval, measured by the MRR@10 metric, varies between <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="(0.565,0.919)" id="S6.SS1.p1.m1"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.565</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.919</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0.565,0.919)</annotation></semantics></math> --> (0.565,0.919)(0.565,0.919), as detailed in Table [6](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.2 Retrievers Results ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"). This variation represents approximately <!-- MathML: <math alttext="35.4\%" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S6.SS1.p1.m2"><semantics><mrow><mn>35.4</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">35.4\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 35.4%35.4\%. It is important to highlight that the RAG’s performance is directly influenced by the quality of the retriever. Figure [12](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S6.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 6.1 Retriever Score versus Performance ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") shows the relationship between the retrieval metric MRR@10 metric and the degradation score for the studied retrieval methods.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/piau_fig.png)Figure 12: Retriever effectiveness vs RAG Performance. <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="x" id="S6.F12.m4"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> --> xx axis is the MRR@10 metric and <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" alttext="y" intent=":literal" id="S6.F12.m5"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> --> yy axis is the degradation (where <!-- MathML: <math display="inline" intent=":literal" alttext="0" id="S6.F12.m6"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> --> 00 is the perfect scenario) score.

### 6.2 Input Size versus Performance

Table 7: Performance of number of chunks retrieved with gpt-4.

We observed that the best performance was achieved with the retrieval of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="3" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S6.SS2.p1.m1"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> --> 33 chunks using the retrieve-and-rerank strategy, as shown in Table [7](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 6.2 Input Size versus Performance ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"). The use of a reranker (Figure [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 5.1.5 Reranker ‣ 5.1 Retrievers ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator")) showed improved information retrieval in our tests. With this same configuration, the Gemini Pro achieved performance similar to gpt-4, as indicated in Table [8](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S6.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 6.2 Input Size versus Performance ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator").

Table 8: Performance of best retriever RAG.

Despite achieving perfect recall for <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" display="inline" alttext="9" id="S6.SS2.p2.m1"><semantics><mn>9</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9</annotation></semantics></math> --> 99 chunks, as evidenced in Table [6](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.2 Retrievers Results ‣ 5 Advanced Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"), using an input with <!-- MathML: <math intent=":literal" alttext="9000" display="inline" id="S6.SS2.p2.m2"><semantics><mn>9000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">9000</annotation></semantics></math> --> 90009000 tokens, <!-- MathML: <math alttext="6000" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S6.SS2.p2.m3"><semantics><mn>6000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6000</annotation></semantics></math> --> 60006000 more than the best scenario (<!-- MathML: <math alttext="3" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S6.SS2.p2.m4"><semantics><mn>3</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3</annotation></semantics></math> --> 33 chunks), did not result in the best performance. As discussed in Section [4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S4.SS2 "4.2 Long Context ‣ 4 Introductory Experiments ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"), the quality of RAG is directly related to the input size and the position where the answer is located. Therefore, the final results confirm the observations made in our experiments.

Moreover, from a cost perspective, it is crucial to avoid overloading the LLM with a large number of input tokens, as the cost is also based on the amount of input text.

It is important to note that the results obtained in this study cannot be considered as a generalization for other datasets. Exploratory Data Analysis and the use of good retriever practices, as presented in [[34](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#bib.bib34 "")], are always a solid path to achieving good results.

### 6.3 Final Results

Despite this work being grounded in a single dataset, it is always crucial to emphasize the importance of data quality. In a simplified manner, as illustrated in Figure [13](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S6.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ 6.3 Final Results ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator"), data quality in RAG can be divided into Input, Retriever, and Evaluation.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/core_points_RAG.png)Figure 13: Core Points in RAG.

- •     Input: How are the queries formulated? Are they synthetic or generic? What is the application’s purpose? Building a RAG for a chatbot differs significantly from constructing a RAG for extracting information from a long and complex document.

- •     Retriever: How do the data behave in information retrieval? Are the queries strongly linked by keywords in the text? What is the cosine similarity of query-to-query, query-to-document, and document-to-document?

- •     Evaluation: How are the data measured? Defining metrics and success rates, as in the first experiment, is always a safe path to avoid biases. Build the evaluation system before testing, avoiding bias.

In conclusion, the main contribution of this work was to identify and present the best possible configuration of techniques and parameters for a RAG application. Figure [14](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#S6.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ 6.3 Final Results ‣ 6 Conclusions ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") provides a summarized overview of the end-to-end experiment results for the discussed approaches, and the best practices recommended by this study achieve a final accuracy of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="98.61\%" display="inline" intent=":literal" id="S6.SS3.p3.m1"><semantics><mrow><mn>98.61</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">98.61\%</annotation></semantics></math> --> 98.61%98.61\%, representing an improvement of <!-- MathML: <math alttext="40.73" intent=":literal" display="inline" id="S6.SS3.p3.m2"><semantics><mn>40.73</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40.73</annotation></semantics></math> --> 40.7340.73 percentage points compared to the baseline.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/final_results.png)Figure 14: RAG Performance: Performance evolution on the Harry Potter dataset, where an accuracy of 100% is considered the relative maximum.

### 6.4 Future Work

We will expand our search to cover additional data sets, preferably those containing real data that already have questions and the reference documents for the answers. By using such datasets, we intend to explore techniques related to segmentation and chunk construction, as elaborated in Appendix B, Section [B](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#A2 "Appendix B Sentence Window ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator").

## Appendix B Sentence Window

There are a wide variety of techniques available for dealing with RAG and new approaches are constantly emerging. In this work we highlight the main existing strategies, although we have also explored others, such as the RAG Sentence Window approach.

The sentence window chunk constitutes a strategy embedded in the llama-index11 1 <https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/examples/node_postprocessor/MetadataReplacementDemo.html>, which employs the small-to-large approach. The entire chunk retrieval process is based on cosine similarity. Initially, a single sentence is retrieved, followed by expanding (window) around the retrieved sentence to construct a more extensive chunk. This method implies that the most relevant context is always centered and retrieved first, as opposed to being at the edges of a chunk boundary. Figure [15](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#A2.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ Appendix B Sentence Window ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator") illustrates the comparison between naive chunks and those obtained through the "sentence window" strategy.

![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1/pics/sentence-window_chunk_2.png)Figure 15: Comparison between the naive chunking and small to big strategies, where the latter initially retrieves a single sentence and then performs windowing with padding on both sides.

Despite being a promising technique, the results on our dataset were inferior to the naive strategy, as indicated in Table [9](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.07883v1#A2.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix B Sentence Window ‣ The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator").

Table 9: Performance of the RAG Sentence Window.

Our hypothesis for the low performance includes:

1. 1.     The construction of the question and answer occurred after the "chunk" cut, so there is no answer between two chunks.

2. 2.     Embedding sentence by sentence in the Harry Potter book causes ambiguity: there are multiple sentences with the name Harry Potter, which adds a significant challenge to the step of retrieving the correct sentence.

THE CHRONICLES OF RAG: THE RETRIEVER, THE CHUNK

AND THE

GENERATOR

PREPRINT

∗Paulo Finardi

∗Leonardo Avila

Rodrigo Castaldoni

Pedro Gengo

Celio Larcher

Marcos Piau

Pablo Costa

Vinicius Caridá

22h, Brazil

email: {pfinardi, leonardo.bernardi.avila, castaldoniro, pedro.gengo.lourenco,

celiolarcher, marcos.piau.vieira, pablo.botton.costa, vfcarida}@gmail.com

∗

Both authors contributed equally to this research.

ABSTRACT

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) has become one of the most popular paradigms for enabling  
LLMs to access external data, and also as a mechanism for grounding to mitigate against halluci-  
nations. When implementing RAG you can face several challenges like effective integration of  
retrieval models, efficient representation learning, data diversity, computational efficiency optimiza-  
tion, evaluation, and quality of text generation. Given all these challenges, every day a new technique  
to improve RAG appears, making it unfeasible to experiment with all combinations for your prob-  
lem. In this context, this paper presents good practices to implement, optimize, and evaluate RAG  
for the Brazilian Portuguese language, focusing on the establishment of a simple pipeline for in-  
ference and experiments. We explored a diverse set of methods to answer questions about the first  
Harry Potter book. To generate the answers we used the OpenAI’s

gpt-4, gpt-4-1106-preview,

gpt-3.5-turbo-1106, and Google’s Gemini Pro. Focusing on the quality of the retriever, our  
approach achieved an improvement of MRR@10 by 35.4% compared to the baseline. When opti-  
mizing the input size in the application, we observed that it is possible to further enhance it by 2.4%.  
Finally, we present the complete architecture of the RAG with our recommendations. As result, we  
moved from a baseline of 57.88% to a maximum relative score of 98.61%.

1

Introduction

The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has changed the way we approach Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications.  
Their ability to answer different user queries in different domains allow these models to show a notable performance  
in a wide range of tasks like translation, summarizing, question answering, and many others [\[1\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)However, there are  
a lot of open challenges when it comes to problems that require answers based on updated information, and external  
data, that were not available in the training data.

In order to overcome this challenge, a technique called Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) [\[2\] ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)was developed.  
This approach aims to solve the limitation of the need for external data, by fetching and incorporating this information  
in the prompt. With this, the model can generate more cohesive answers about subjects and data not seen during the  
training, decreasing the occurrence of hallucinations [\[3\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)Nevertheless, this approach adds a new layer of challenges  
since it requires the development of a trustworthy retriever pipeline, given that the quality of the final answer can be  
highly affected if the retrieved text is not relevant to the user query [\[4\].](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)

The landscape of RAG is rapidly expanding, with a constant influx of new papers introducing diverse implementations  
[\[5\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)Each of these variants proposes technical modifications or enhancements, such as different retrieval mechanisms,  
augmentation techniques, or fine-tuning methodologies. This proliferation, while a testament to the field’s dynamism,

arXiv:2401.07883v1 \[cs.LG\] 15 Jan 2024

 link to page 2 link to page 15 link to page 13 link to page 13 link to page 13 link to page 13 

The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator

PREPRINT

presents a substantial challenge for AI practitioners. The task of methodically experimenting with, and critically  
evaluating, each variant’s performance, scalability, and applicability becomes increasingly complex.

In this paper, we present a comprehensive series of experiments focused on the application of RAG specifically tailored  
for Brazilian Portuguese. Our research delves into evaluating various retrieval techniques, including both sparse and  
dense retrievers. Additionally, we explore two chunking strategies (naive and sentence window) to optimize the  
integration of retrieved information into the generation process. We also investigate the impact of the positioning of  
documents within the prompt, analyzing how this influences the overall quality and relevance of the generated content.  
Finally, our experiments extend to comparing the performance of different LLMs, notably GPT-4 and Gemini, in their  
ability to effectively incorporate the retrieved information and produce coherent, contextually accurate responses. This  
paper aims to provide valuable insights and practical guidelines for implementing RAG in Brazilian Portuguese.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 1) we propose a methodology to prepare a dataset in a format that  
allows quantifying the quality of the different steps in an RAG system. 2) We proposed a metric (maximum relative  
score) that allow us to direct quantify the existent gap between each approach and a perfect RAG system. 3) We discuss  
and compare different implementations, showing good practices and optimizations that can be used when developing  
a RAG system.

2

Data Preparation

The chosen dataset was the first Harry Potter book in its Brazilian Portuguese version. This choice is motivated  
since it is a well known book, and both the

Gemini Pro and OpenAI models can answer general questions on the

subject. Additionally, over the application of the standard ChatGPT tokenizer

cl100k\_base, we observed that there

are approximately 140, 000 tokens in total, allowing the creation of prompts containing the entire book. Following, a  
dataset consisting of questions and corresponding answers was developed, with both question and answer generated  
by the gpt-4 model and based on a reference chunk.

Figure 1: From a large document (book), chunks were created, and for each chunk, a question and an answer were  
generated using

gpt-4, where the answer is contained within the chunk.

Figure [1 ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#2)shows the data preparation process. Initially, the dataset was break into chunks with 1000 tokens each, without  
overlapping, resulting in 140 chunks. Then, using the prompt described in Appendix [A, ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#15)a {question, answer} pair  
was created for each chunk in the style of the

SQuAD dataset [\[6\], ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)meaning that the answer to the question is present

within the reference text (chunk).

3

How to Evaluate

The contextual comparison of two text samples is not a straightforward task. For instance, despite the sentence1 =  
"Brazil has won 5 FIFA World Cup titles."

, and sentence2 = "Brazil is the five-time champion of the FIFA World

Cup."

(both sentences translated into English for convenience) convey the same meaning, traditional metrics such as

BLEU [\[7\] ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)and ROUGE [\[8\] ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)score may not be able to capture such similarity. Specifically, for the example cited:

•

BLEU score \[sentence1, sentence2\] = 0.33

•

ROUGE score \[sentence1, sentence2\] = 0.22

Therefore, an approach widely used in the literature is to employ

gpt-4 to provide a score based on a given prompt, a

concept similar to what was done in the G-Eval work [\[9\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)In this work, a scoring system divided into 5 categories to  
compare two texts was devised, with scores defined as following (translated into English for convenience):

 link to page 15 link to page 3 link to page 2 link to page 3 link to page 2 link to page 13 

The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator

PREPRINT

• score 1: The answer has no relation to the reference.

• score 3: The answer has little relevance but is not aligned with the reference.

• score 5: The answer has moderate relevance but contains inaccuracies.

• score 7: The answer is aligned with the reference but has minor omissions.

• score 10: The answer is completely accurate and aligns perfectly with the reference.

The prompt used in the evaluation is shown in Appendix [A. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#15)Our approach uses a one-shot technique for each scoring  
category. Although, we believe that the evaluation could become more robust and deterministic with the addition of  
more few-shot examples for each scoring category, these possible variations were not explored in this work.

3.1

Relative Maximum Score

In order to assess performance variation for the followings experiments, we created a metric called the relative max-  
imum score, which corresponds to the score given by a model when evaluating the correct combination of question  
and chunk for all pairs of a given dataset. Through this approach, it is possible to obtain the maximum score that an  
evaluated LLM could reach for a RAG system.

The Table [1 ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#3)presents results for the custom dataset created in Section [2, ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#2)by using different LLMs to generate the  
answer and the

gpt-4 score system previously defined.

Table 1: Relative maximum score in 140 questions from the created QA Harry Potter dataset.

average points. This points out that, even with a perfect retriever strategy, the RAG system is not able to achieve a  
perfect score in this dataset by using these LLM models.

For now on, all experiments in this study were assessed in terms of both the relative maximum and the percentage  
degradation with respect to the relative maximum, as defined in Equation [1.](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#3)

With this score, we are able to address the problems regarding the retriever system itself, instead of having a vague  
idea of where is the main gap of our pipeline.

4

Introductory Experiments

In this section, we will establish a baseline for the metrics defined in Section [3\. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#2)Additionally, we will apply tech-  
niques of lower complexity and compare the results with the baseline. It’s worth noting that we did not explore  
prompt engineering techniques, although we are aware that prompt engineering has a direct impact on performance,  
as demonstrated in [\[10\].](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)

4.1

Baseline: no context

We are aware that LLMs are trained on a massive dataset that covers virtually the entire web. This circumstance,  
coupled with the popularity of the Harry Potter universe, forms a robust hypothesis for testing questions in isolation  
on OpenAI models. The answer for basic questions such as "Who is Harry Potter?", "Who killed Dumbledore?", and  
"What are Harry Potter’s main friends?", ChatGPT were correctly answered with precision. However, we observed  
that when dealing with more detailed questions, the performance was only reasonable. Below are two examples of  
detailed questions (translated into English for convenience):

Long Context

In comparison to the GPT 1 and 2 models [\[11, 12\], ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)which handle up to 1024 input tokens, the

The specific architecture of

gpt-4 has not been disclosed, but it is believed that this model has not been pre-trained

with a 128k token input context [\[13\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)Perhaps a post-pre-training technique could have been used, which would have

RAG Naive

Initially, a straightforward approach for RAG will be done using the llama-index [\[19\], ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)employing all default hyper-

5

Advanced Experiments

The studies and experiments outlined in section [4 ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#3)have shown unsatisfactory performance, marked by a degradation  
of at least 20% compared to the peak relative performance. Therefore, in this section, we explore various retrieval  
approaches for the RAG, recognizing that the quality of the retriever is a crucial factor in enhancing performance for  
this type of problem. We conducted an evaluation covering both sparse and dense search, a hybrid method, and even  
a multi-stage architecture using a reranker.

In pursuit of code debugging flexibility and easier customization at each stage, we chose not to utilize an RAG frame-  
work (like LangChain or Llama-Index). For a comprehensive guide on debugging RAG and more details about retrieval  
systems, refer to [\[20\] ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)and [\[21\].](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)

5.1

Retrievers

When deploying retrieval systems, it is essential to achieve a balance between “effectiveness” (How good are the  
results returned?

) and “efficiency” (How much time it takes to return the results? or How much resources are used in

terms of disk/RAM/GPU?

). This balance ensures that latency, result quality, and computational budget remain within

our application’s required limits. This work will exclusively focus on effectiveness measures to quantify the retrievers  
methods quality.

In our retriever experiments, the evaluation strategy centers around assessing how well the retriever performs in re-  
trieving relevant information based on each given query qi. To achieve this, we employ the concept of recall. It is  
defined as the fraction of the relevant documents for a given query qi that are successfully retrieved in a ranked list  
R [\[21\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)This metric is based on binary relevance judgments, assuming that documents are either relevant or not [\[21\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)In this paper, each chunk is considered a document and only the respective chunk di is considered relevant to the query  
qi. While recall is easy to interpret, it does not consider the specific rank positions in which the relevant chunk appears  
in R.

To overcome this limitation, we introduce Reciprocal Rank (RR) into our analysis. In this metric, the rank of the  
first relevant document to the query in R is used to compute the RR score [\[21\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)Therefore, Reciprocal Rank offers a  
more nuanced evaluation by assigning a higher value when the relevant chunk is returned in the early positions of our  
retrievers given the respective query.

Recall and Reciprocal Rank were evaluated at a specific cutoff so the measures are presented as R@k and MRR@k.  
For each query, its results are evaluated and their mean serves as an aggregated measure of effectiveness of a given  
retriever method. The retrievers are introduced below.

In the category of sparse retrievers, we emphasize the BM25, a technique grounded in statistical weighting to assess  
relevance between search terms and documents. BM25 employs a scoring function that takes into account term  
frequency and document length, offering an efficient approach for retrieving pertinent information and is typically  
used as a strong baseline. However, it is exact-match based and can be powerless when query and document are  
relevant to each other but has no common words.

On the other hand, when exploring dense retrievers, we often encounter approaches based on the called bi-encoder  
design [\[22\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)The bi-encoder independently encodes queries and documents, creating separate vector representations  
before calculating similarity. An advantage of this approach is that it can be initialized ‘offline’: document embeddings  
can be precomputed, leaving only the query embedding being calculated at search time, reducing latency.

The hybrid search technique aims to leverage the best of both sparse and dense search approaches. Given a question,  
both searches are conducted in parallel, generating two lists of candidate documents to answer it. The challenge then  
lies in combining the two results in the best possible way, ensuring that the final hybrid list surpasses the individual  
searches. Essentially, we can conceptualize it as a voting system, where each searcher casts a vote on the relevance of  
a document to a given query, and in the end, the opinions are combined to produce a better result.

The multi-stage search architecture is based on the retrieve-and-rerank pipeline. In the first stage, a retriever with good  
recall is typically used to perform an initial filtering of the documents to be returned. From this narrowed-down list,  
these candidate documents are then sent to a second stage, which involves higher computational complexity, to rerank  
them and enhance the final effectiveness of the system.

Next, we provide more details about each retriever used.

5.1.1

BM25

Due to the user-friendly nature of BM25, its inclusion as a retriever method is always a welcome addition in RAG  
evaluations. A study that aligns with the same reasoning, albeit for a different application, can be found in [\[23\], ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)which  
illustrates the benefits of employing this algorithm to establish a robust baseline. Given that our data shares similarities  
with the

SQuAD dataset, it is expected that many words from the query would be present in the chunk, contributing to

the favorable effectiveness of BM25.

In the BM25 ranking function, k1 and b are parameters shaping term saturation and document length normalization,  
respectively. The BM25 formula integrates these parameters to score the relevance of a document to a query, offering  
flexibility in adjusting k1 and b for improving effectiveness in different retrieval scenarios.

5.1.2

ADA-002

OpenAI does not disclose extensive details about the ADA-002 architecture; however, we employed this model in  
retrieval as the presented bi-encoder design (Figure [5): ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#7)vector representations were constructed for all available chunks,  
and for each input query, its embedding was computed at search time. Subsequently, the similarity between the  
question and chunk were assessed using cosine similarity.

Figure 5: Bi-Encoder Architecture

Since we have no further details about ADA-002 we will refer to this approach only as dense retriever.

5.1.3

Custom ADA-002

The Custom ADA-002 approach was also utilized in the dense retriever configuration presented in Section [5.1.2. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#7)However, embedding customization played a key role in our attempt to enhance the overall representation.

Embedding customization is not limited solely to OpenAI’s embeddings; it is a technique applicable to other embed-  
dings of the same kind. There is a significant variety of approaches to optimize a matrix, with one of them being

 link to page 14 link to page 8 link to page 8 

The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator

PREPRINT

the application of Multiple Negative Ranking Loss, as presented in the article "Efficient Natural Language Response  
Suggestion for Smart Reply," Section 4.4 [\[26\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)However, given our current focus on simplicity, we will reserve the  
exploration of this technique for future work. At this moment, we choose to utilize the Mean Squared Error (MSE)  
Loss.

For the fine-tuning stage, it is necessary to have two types of samples:

• positives: \[questioni, chunki, label = 1\]

• negatives: \[questioni, chunkj, label = −1\], for i ̸= j

Often, as is the case with our dataset, only positive examples are available. However, through a simple and random  
shuffling, it is possible to generate negative examples. Demonstrating confidence in transfer learning, we found that  
a few examples were sufficient. Our final dataset consisted of approximately 400 examples, maintaining a 1 : 3 ratio  
between positive and negative examples.

The hyperparameters that exert the most significant impact on performance include the learning rate, batch size, and  
the number of dimensions in the projection matrix. The ADA-002 model has 1536 dimensions, and the projection  
matrix is of size 1536 × N, where N ∈ 1024, 2048, 4096\. In our experiments, we observed that 2048 dimensions  
resulted in the best accuracy.

This type of fine-tuning requires low GPU resources, with a training time of approximately 5 minutes using the A100  
GPU. The model itself is straightforward, consisting of a matrix with dropout (to mitigate overfitting), followed by the  
hyperbolic tangent activation function, which provided additional accuracy gains in the training set.

5.1.5

Reranker

The fundamental idea underlying multi-stage ranking is to divide document ranking into a sequence of stages. After  
an initial retrieval, which usually involves a sparse retriever or dense retriever, each subsequent stage re-evaluates and  
reranks the set of candidates forwarded from the preceding stage. Figure [9 ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#9)represents a multi-stage pipeline where  
Pyserini BM25 performs the first stage and the candidate chunks are then re-evaluated by the reranker. After that, the  
final reranked list called retrieved chunks is presented as final result formed by k chunks.

Transformers-based models are commonly employed as rerankers, leveraging their capability to enhance the effective-  
ness of information retrieval systems by capturing intricate relationships and contextual information within documents

The initial utilization of transformers within a multi-stage ranking framework was presented in the study [\[28\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)Their  
proposed model, known as monoBERT, transforms the ranking process into a relevance classification problem. It  
achieves this by sorting texts based on the conditional probability P (Relevant = 1 | di; q), where q is the query and  
di represents documents [\[21\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)The model simultaneously processes both queries and documents. This simultaneous  
processing leads to a more enriched interaction between them, often resulting in improved effectiveness [\[29\], \[30\]. ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)However, this neural models have a substantial number of parameters and the scoring of query-document pairs occurs  
at inference time. This, in turn, increases computational costs and latency. This kind of model is also known by  
cross-encoder. Refer to Figure [10 ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#10)for an illustration of the query-document pair processing.

In the other hand, monoT5 is a sequence-to-sequence reranker [\[31\] ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)that uses T5 models [\[32\] ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#14)to generate relevance  
scores between a pair of query and document. T5 models treat all tasks as text-to-text, requiring some adaptations  
for the query/document similarity task. During training, the format

'Query: {query} Document: {document}

Relevant:' is used, with labels yes if the document is relevant to the query, and no otherwise. At inference time, the

false and true. Figure [11 ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#10)contains an illustration of the monoT5 architecture’s inference process.

6

Conclusions

The implementation of RAG systems faces challenges such as the effective integration of retrieval models, efficient  
representation learning, the diversity of data, the optimization of computational efficiency, evaluation, and text genera-  
tion quality. Faced with these constantly evolving obstacles, this article proposes best practices for the implementation,  
optimization, and evaluation of RAG on a Brazilian Portuguese dataset, focusing on a simplified pipeline for inference  
and experimentation.

So far, we have introduced the main components and methods along with their results and gaps. In this section, we will  
discuss key points that contribute to the performance improvement in RAG applications. We will start by discussing  
the relationship between the quality of the retriever and the achieved performance, in which our approach showed  
a significant improvement of MRR@10 by 35.4% compared to the baseline. Next, we will address the impact of  
input size on performance. In this domain, we observed that it is possible to enhance the best information retrieval  
strategy by 2.4% through input size optimization. Finally, we will present the complete architecture of RAG with  
our recommendations. When evaluating the final accuracy of our approach, we reached 98.61%, representing an  
improvement of 40.73 in less degradation score compared to the baseline.

6.3

Final Results

Despite this work being grounded in a single dataset, it is always crucial to emphasize the importance of data quality.  
In a simplified manner, as illustrated in Figure [13, ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#12)data quality in RAG can be divided into Input, Retriever, and  
Evaluation.

Figure 13: Core Points in RAG.

• Input: How are the queries formulated? Are they synthetic or generic? What is the application’s purpose?

Building a RAG for a chatbot differs significantly from constructing a RAG for extracting information from  
a long and complex document.

• Retriever: How do the data behave in information retrieval? Are the queries strongly linked by keywords in

the text? What is the cosine similarity of query-to-query, query-to-document, and document-to-document?

• Evaluation: How are the data measured? Defining metrics and success rates, as in the first experiment, is

always a safe path to avoid biases. Build the evaluation system before testing, avoiding bias.

In conclusion, the main contribution of this work was to identify and present the best possible configuration of tech-  
niques and parameters for a RAG application. Figure [14 ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#13)provides a summarized overview of the end-to-end experi-  
ment results for the discussed approaches, and the best practices recommended by this study achieve a final accuracy  
of 98.61%, representing an improvement of 40.73 percentage points compared to the baseline.

The Chronicles of RAG: The Retriever, the Chunk and the Generator

PREPRINT

B

Sentence Window

There are a wide variety of techniques available for dealing with RAG and new approaches are constantly emerging. In  
this work we highlight the main existing strategies, although we have also explored others, such as the RAG Sentence  
Window approach.

The sentence window chunk constitutes a strategy embedded in the llama-inde[x1, ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#16)which employs the small-to-large  
approach. The entire chunk retrieval process is based on cosine similarity. Initially, a single sentence is retrieved,  
followed by expanding (window) around the retrieved sentence to construct a more extensive chunk. This method  
implies that the most relevant context is always centered and retrieved first, as opposed to being at the edges of a  
chunk boundary. Figure [15 ](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#16)illustrates the comparison between naive chunks and those obtained through the "sentence  
window" strategy.

Figure 15: Comparison between the naive chunking and small to big strategies, where the latter initially retrieves a  
single sentence and then performs windowing with padding on both sides.

Despite being a promising technique, the results on our dataset were inferior to the naive strategy, as indicated in Table  
[9.](1793495369636-bed9d33a-9fde-4d38-9cd7-851726a800b1-file116573.html#16)

1\. The construction of the question and answer occurred after the "chunk" cut, so there is no answer between

two chunks.

2\. Embedding sentence by sentence in the Harry Potter book causes ambiguity: there are multiple sentences

The **United States secretary of energy** is the head of the [United States Department of Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Energy "United States Department of Energy"), a member of the [Cabinet of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") and fifteenth in the [presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession"). The position was created on October 1, 1977, when President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") signed the [Department of Energy Organization Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Energy_Organization_Act "Department of Energy Organization Act"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-2) establishing the department. Originally, the secretary and the department focused on energy production and regulation. Over time, the emphasis shifted to developing technology for more efficient energy sources and energy education. After the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), the department's attention also turned to [radioactive waste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_waste "Radioactive waste") disposal and environmental quality maintenance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-3)

Former [secretary of defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Defense "United States Secretary of Defense") [James Schlesinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_R._Schlesinger "James R. Schlesinger") was the first secretary of energy. As a Republican nominated by Democratic president Jimmy Carter, Schlesinger’s appointment remains the only instance of a president choosing a member of another political party for the position. Schlesinger is also the only secretary to be dismissed from the post.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-4) [Hazel O'Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazel_R._O'Leary "Hazel R. O'Leary"), [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton")’s first secretary of energy, was the first female and first African American to hold the position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-5) The first [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans "Hispanic and Latino Americans") to serve as energy secretary was Clinton’s second energy secretary, [Federico Peña](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Peña "Federico Peña"). [Spencer Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spencer_Abraham "Spencer Abraham") became the first [Arab American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Americans "Arab Americans") to hold the position on January 20, 2001, under President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"). [Steven Chu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Chu "Steven Chu"), appointed on January 20, 2009, under President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama"), became the first [Asian American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Americans "Asian Americans") to hold the position. Chu also served as the longest-serving secretary of energy and was the first individual to join the Cabinet after having received a Nobel Prize.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-6) Former Michigan governor, [Jennifer Granholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Granholm "Jennifer Granholm"), confirmed on February 25, 2021 under President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"), was the second woman to lead the Department of Energy.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-7) [Chris Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Wright "Chris Wright") is the current secretary of energy under the Trump administration, confirmed on February, 3, 2025.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-8)

## Nuclear weapons

In addition to responsibilities related to generation and use of energy, the secretary is the most senior official other than the president of the United States or secretary of defense with primary responsibility for the nation's approximately 3,800 viable nuclear weapons. This arrangement is intended to maintain full civilian control over strategic weapons, except as directed by the president for specific military uses.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-9) The department of energy is responsible for the building, maintenance, and disposal of all nuclear weapons within the United States' arsenal in addition to safeguarding these weapons when they are not actively deployed in military service.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-10) Under the terms of several successive treaties, most recently New START, the United States has reduced its strategic arsenal to 1,500 deployed weapons. Consequently, many older legacy weapons systems have been dismantled or scheduled for dismantlement, with their core radioactive fuel - generally plutonium - being reprocessed into reactor-grade or space exploration fuel.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Energy#cite_note-11)
